title: Job 28:1–11
context: Job 28:1–11 opens the hymn to wisdom, whose speaker is debated (Job, or the narrator in an interlude). Job’s discourse begins in 27:1, and nothing in the text marks a new speaker before Job is introduced again in 29:1, so many read chapter 28 as Job’s words. Others read it as an interlude by the narrator that stands between the speeches. The poem is not a speech by one of the friends, and it does not settle Job’s case ahead of the LORD’s speeches (chapters 38–41) or his verdict (42:7). The first stanza praises human skill in mining. People dig for silver, gold, iron, and copper, push into darkness, sink shafts far from where anyone lives, and bring hidden treasure to light along paths that no bird or wild animal knows. The picture prepares for the question in verse 12: humans can find what is hidden in the earth, but where will wisdom be found? Both traditions read this stanza as celebrating God-given human ability while setting up its limits.

verses.text: “Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold which they refine.
verses.arminianNotes: The poem begins by saying there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined. Arminian readers see an admiring look at human skill, which God gave to people as part of their calling to work and explore his world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the opening as a picture of human ability under God’s common grace. Both traditions note that the poem starts with what people can find in order to ask, by contrast, what they cannot find on their own.

verses.text: Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted out of the ore.
verses.arminianNotes: Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore. Arminians see the poem continuing its catalog of human achievement, describing the hard work of drawing useful metals out of rock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a realistic picture of ancient mining and metalwork. Both traditions treat the details as illustration, preparing for the poem’s question about where wisdom is found.

verses.text: Man sets an end to darkness, and searches out, to the furthest bound, the stones of obscurity and of thick darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: Humans set an end to darkness and search the furthest stones of gloom. Arminian readers see the boldness of miners, who go into places no light reaches in order to find what is hidden there.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see human curiosity and persistence as gifts from the Creator. Both traditions note that darkness in this poem marks the edge of human reach, which wisdom itself lies beyond.

verses.text: He breaks open a shaft away from where people live. They are forgotten by the foot. They hang far from men, they swing back and forth.
verses.arminianNotes: The miner opens a shaft far from where people live and hangs and swings far from others. Arminians see a vivid picture of the danger and isolation of the work, which shows how far people will go for treasure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Some details of this verse are difficult in Hebrew and are translated in different ways, so both traditions hold the specific picture loosely while agreeing on its main point: human effort reaches remarkable depths.

verses.text: As for the earth, out of it comes bread. Underneath it is turned up as it were by fire.
verses.arminianNotes: Bread comes from the surface of the earth, while underneath it is turned up as by fire. Arminian readers see a contrast between farming above and mining below, both of which show how people draw riches out of the ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the earth as a storehouse that God placed under human care. Both traditions read the fire as either the heat of the earth or the methods miners used, and hold that question open.

verses.text: Sapphires come from its rocks. It has dust of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Its rocks hold sapphires and its dust holds gold. Arminians see the hidden wealth of creation, which humans have learned to search out and value. The word rendered sapphires may refer to lapis lazuli.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the riches of creation as testimony to the Creator’s generosity. Both traditions note that the poem lists treasures so it can later say that wisdom is worth more than all of them.

verses.text: That path no bird of prey knows, neither has the falcon’s eye seen it.
verses.arminianNotes: No bird of prey knows that path, and the falcon’s eye has not seen it. Arminian readers see the point that miners go where even the keenest-eyed creatures cannot follow, underground and out of sight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as stressing the hiddenness of the miner’s path. Both traditions note that verse 21 will echo this language when it says wisdom is hidden even from the birds of the sky.

verses.text: The proud animals have not trodden it, nor has the fierce lion passed by there.
verses.arminianNotes: Proud animals have not walked there, and the fierce lion has not passed by. Arminians see the poem adding that even the strongest animals have never reached the places humans have opened up.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as completing the picture of human reach beyond the animal world. Both traditions treat it as preparation for the turn in verse 12, where human reach itself meets its limit.

verses.text: He puts his hand on the flinty rock, and he overturns the mountains by the roots.
verses.arminianNotes: The miner puts his hand on flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots. Arminian readers see poetic exaggeration that honors the power of human labor, which can reshape the land itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the language as celebrating what people can do with the abilities God gave them. Both traditions note that similar language is used of God elsewhere in Job (9:5), which may hint that human power is real but derived.

verses.text: He cuts out channels among the rocks. His eye sees every precious thing.
verses.arminianNotes: He cuts channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing. Arminians see human skill and attention finding what is valuable in the earth, a real achievement the poem respects.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions note the contrast the poem is building: the miner’s eye sees every precious thing in the rock, yet in verses 23–24 only God sees where wisdom is.

verses.text: He binds the streams that they don’t trickle. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light.
verses.arminianNotes: He binds the streams so they do not trickle and brings hidden things to light. Arminian readers see the summit of human achievement in the stanza: people can control water and uncover what was concealed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the line as closing the first stanza on a high note. Both traditions read it as the setup for the question that follows, since bringing hidden things to light does not bring wisdom to light.
